Edvard Munch. The Norwegian painter and printmaker lived from eighteen sixty-three to nineteen forty-four. His deeply personal, psychologically intense works anticipated Expressionism and influenced generations of artists. Though born in Scandinavia, his work resonated strongly with German Expressionists, and he maintained lifelong connections to Berlin. His visceral images of anxiety, alienation, and mortality remain icons of modernist art's emotional extremes.

Munch was born in Løten, Norway in eighteen sixty-three. He spent formative years in Oslo and moved frequently between Scandinavia, Berlin, and Paris throughout his restless career. He created The Scream in eighteen ninety-three, arguably the twentieth century's most iconic image of psychological distress, existential terror, and modern alienation. The image is now instantly recognizable and globally reproduced.

He exhibited in Berlin in eighteen ninety-two, and German audiences embraced his work immediately as a revelation of new emotional possibilities. Conservative Scandinavian critics dismissed it as degenerate. He explored recurring themes of death, separation, jealousy, loneliness, and mortality through distorted figures, vibrant dissonant colour, and energetic brushwork.

Munch worked across painting, printmaking including lithography, woodcuts, and etchings, and sculpture, achieving technical mastery in each medium and experimenting with artistic innovation continuously. He suffered from alcoholism, depression, and recurrent mental health crises. He spent years at a mental health clinic from nineteen oh eight to nineteen oh nine treating nervous exhaustion and paranoia before resuming work.

His artistic legacy bridges Impressionism, Symbolism, and Expressionism, making him a crucial transitional figure. His work bridges Symbolism with emotional and psychological content and Expressionism with distorted forms and raw emotion. Modern psychology, existentialism, and psychoanalysis, all emerging during his lifetime, found visual expression in Munch's exploration of anxiety, desire, and the unconscious mind. He returned to Norway in his later years, achieved national recognition as a major artist, and died in Oslo in nineteen forty-four with his reputation fully rehabilitated.
